title: Web Development with React
summary: Learn to build modern web interfaces with React: components and props, state and events, lists and conditional rendering, effects and data fetching, forms, routing and deployment.
audience: Learners who know HTML, CSS and basic JavaScript and want to build interactive web apps

lessons.title: Why React and how it thinks

body.p: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components: small, reusable pieces such as a button, a product card or a whole page. Instead of changing the page step by step, you describe what the interface should look like for the current data, and React updates the screen efficiently when the data changes.

list: Know HTML, CSS and modern JavaScript: arrow functions, destructuring, the spread operator (...), array methods such as map and filter, modules and promises.
Install Node.js, then create a project with a build tool such as Vite: npm create vite@latest my-app, choosing React.
Run npm install, then npm run dev to start a local development server that reloads as you edit.

body.p: React powers many large web apps, and the same ideas carry over to React Native for mobile apps. Its ecosystem includes routing, data-fetching and testing libraries, and frameworks such as Next.js add server rendering.

Look at a design and draw boxes around each part. A shop page might contain a header, a search box, a product list and product cards. Each box becomes a component, and components nest inside each other.

body.tip: Keep components small and focused. If a component is hard to name, it is probably doing too much.

body.p: A component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX, a syntax that looks like HTML inside JavaScript. Data is passed into components through props (properties), like arguments to a function.

list: Component names start with a capital letter: ProductCard, not productCard.
Curly braces {} insert JavaScript values into JSX: {name}, {price}.
Use className instead of class, because class is a JavaScript keyword.
A component returns one parent element; wrap siblings in a div or an empty fragment <>…</>.
Props are read-only: a component must not change the props it receives.

body.p: Here App renders a ProductCard showing "Calculator" and "R4500". The same component can render any product by passing different props, which is why components are reusable.

body.tip: Destructure props in the parameter list ({ name, price }) so the component shows clearly which data it needs.

body.p: State is data that a component remembers and that can change over time: what a user typed, whether a menu is open, how many times a button was clicked. The useState hook returns the current value and a function to update it. Updating state makes React re-render the component with the new value.
Event handlers such as onClick receive a function. Here each click calls setCount with an updater function, c => c + 1.

A component's state value is fixed for the duration of one render. If a handler calls setCount(count + 1) twice while count is 0, both calls set the value to 0 + 1, so the result is 1, not 2. Using setCount(c => c + 1) twice passes each update the latest value, giving 2. This behaviour was checked with a small JavaScript simulation.

list: Never change state directly (count = 5 or array.push); always call the setter.
For arrays and objects, create new copies: setItems([...items, newItem]).
Lift state up to the nearest common parent when two components need the same data.

body.tip: Ask "does this value change, and does the screen depend on it?" If yes, it is state; if it can be calculated from other values, calculate it instead.

body.p: Real interfaces show lists of data and change what they show depending on conditions. In React you use ordinary JavaScript for both.

With products Exercise book (R350), Calculator (R4500) and Pen (R100), filter keeps items under R1000, so the list shows Exercise book and Pen. If none qualified, the component would return the message instead.

list: map turns each data item into JSX.
Each list item needs a stable, unique key, ideally an ID from the data, so React can track items when the list changes. Avoid using the array index when items can be reordered or deleted.
Conditional rendering uses if statements, the ternary operator (cond ? a : b) or && to show something only when a condition is true.
Derived values, such as the total price (here 4950), should be calculated from state rather than stored separately.

body.tip: If React warns about missing keys, fix it; wrong keys cause strange bugs where inputs show the wrong item's data.

body.p: Rendering should only calculate what to show. Work that reaches outside the component, such as fetching data, timers or subscriptions, goes in the useEffect hook, which runs after React updates the screen.

list: The empty dependency array [] means "run once after the first render".
List every value the effect uses in the dependency array; the effect re-runs when they change.
Always handle loading and error states so users are never left with a blank screen.
Return a clean-up function from an effect to stop timers or subscriptions when the component disappears.

body.p: For larger apps, data-fetching libraries handle caching, retries and loading states for you, and frameworks can fetch data on the server.

body.tip: Never put secret API keys in React code; everything in the browser bundle can be read by users. Call your own server or edge function, which holds the secret.

body.p: Forms in React are usually controlled: each input's value comes from state and onChange updates that state. On submit, call event.preventDefault(), validate the values, show clear errors next to fields, and disable the button while sending.

Single-page apps switch views without reloading the whole page. A routing library maps URLs such as /courses and /courses/42 to components, and links change the URL without a full reload, so the back button and bookmarks still work.

list: Keep files organised by feature, with one main component per file.
Test components with a testing library, simulating clicks and typing as a user would.
Check accessibility: real buttons and labels, keyboard support and good contrast.
npm run build creates optimised static files that can be hosted on services such as GitHub Pages, Netlify or Vercel, or served from your own server.
Measure performance on a low-cost phone; split large bundles and lazy-load rarely used pages.

body.tip: Build a real project, such as a course catalogue with search and favourites, and publish it. A live project teaches more than any tutorial.
